claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a high-temperature single-phase BCC alloy.
The BCC phase stability of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by the Gibbs-free-energy difference between BCC and FCC.
CALPHAD calculations can be used to evaluate BCC–FCC thermodynamic phase stability.
A sufficiently negative ΔG_BCC-FCC stabilizes BCC at high temperature.
Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 has a large or significant negative ΔG_BCC-FCC at high temperature.
Reducing the Al content from the Al7 composition to the stated Al5 composition reduces the BCC–FCC free-energy gap.
Reducing the BCC–FCC free-energy gap shifts equilibrium toward FCC during cooling.
Phase selection proceeds by minimization of Gibbs free energy.
The baseline Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy should remain BCC at high temperature.
The reduced-Al alloy should exhibit a higher FCC fraction or an earlier onset of FCC formation during cooling than the baseline alloy.
The extent of BCC-to-FCC transformation should correlate with CALPHAD-predicted BCC–FCC free-energy differences.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily above approximately 1000 °C.
The thermodynamic prediction is expected to apply when kinetic barriers are not dominant.
Sluggish diffusion is typical of high-entropy alloys and can impede phase transformation.
Rapid-cooling kinetics may prevent a quantitative mapping from calculated ΔG_BCC-FCC to measured phase fractions.
Minor elements and processing-induced defects may cause behavior not captured by the CALPHAD model.
An inert atmosphere minimizes oxidation effects during thermal cycling.
X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy can determine the relative BCC and FCC phase fractions.

contradictions.description: ΔG_BCC-FCC is treated as a signed quantity for which negative values favor BCC, but lowering Al is said to 'reduce' the gap and thereby favor FCC. If 'reduce' means making the signed ΔG smaller, it would become more negative and favor BCC; the intended meaning appears to be reducing its magnitude or making it less negative.

The boundary and uncertainty fields allow lack of correlation to arise from kinetic limitations, whereas the falsification rule treats lack of correlation under controlled cooling as falsifying the thermodynamic mechanism without specifying a near-equilibrium cooling condition or a criterion that excludes kinetic control.
